meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You could not step twice into the same river; for other waters are ever flowing on to you'?
meta.ogDescription: Correctly credited to Heraclitus, but the exact wording is Plato's paraphrase, not his own words. His genuine river fragment (B12) reads otherwise.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 540 – c. 480 BCE · Pre-Socratic philosopher of Ephesus
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Heraclitus in substance — the ever-flowing river is his signature image for a world in constant change — but this exact one-sentence form is Plato’s paraphrase in the Cratylus (402a), here in a public-domain 19th-century English translation. Heraclitus’s one securely genuine river fragment (DK B12) actually reads “other and other waters flow” on those who step in — not “you could not step twice.”

source.heading: The river fragment

docMeta.dd: Public-domain English rendering (Bywater Greek text, late 19th c.)

source.excerpt: “Heraclitus, I believe, says that all things pass and nothing stays, and comparing existing things to the flow of a river, he says you could not step twice into the same river.”
trail: Our earliest source is Plato: in the Cratylus (c. 360 BCE, 402a) Socrates reports that Heraclitus “says you could not step twice into the same river” — the single-sentence form everyone quotes is Plato’s condensation, not a surviving line of Heraclitus’s own.

Heraclitus’s one certifiably genuine river fragment (DK B12), preserved through later writers, actually reads “on those stepping into rivers staying the same, other and other waters flow” — and scholars (Marcovich 1967) argue the “step twice” versions come from a misreading of it, per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

The exact English wording — “other waters are ever flowing on to you” — is a public-domain late-19th-century translation reproduced on Wikiquote; John Burnet’s contemporaneous rendering has “fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you,” as printed in the annotated fragments.
source.excerptNote: That is Plato’s summary. Heraclitus’s own securely genuine river fragment (DK B12) reads instead: “on those stepping into rivers staying the same, other and other waters flow.” The neat “step twice” sentence — and the popular “other waters are ever flowing on to you” tail — is the later, condensed form.
source.rightsNote: The underlying Greek — Plato’s Cratylus and Heraclitus’s fragments — has been in the public domain for millennia, and the specific English wording here is a public-domain translation first printed in the late 19th century, well before 1931. No modern rights attach to this phrasing.

author.name: Heraclitus
author.heading: About Heraclitus
author.metaLine: c. 540 – c. 480 BCE · Pre-Socratic philosopher of Ephesus
author.bio: Heraclitus of Ephesus was a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher active around 500 BCE, remembered for his doctrine that reality is in ceaseless change, held together by the logos. He wrote a single book, now lost; roughly a hundred cryptic fragments survive only as quotations in later authors, earning him the nickname “the Obscure.” The river — into which fresh water is always flowing — became his defining image for a world in permanent flux.

misattribution.heading: What gets blurred
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Heraclitus is essentially right — the flux doctrine and the river are genuinely his. What gets blurred is whose exact words these are and which river line Heraclitus actually wrote.

items.why: The tidy “you could not step twice into the same river” sentence is Plato’s summary of Heraclitus in the Cratylus 402a, not a line from Heraclitus’s own book. His one certifiably genuine river fragment (B12) says “other and other waters flow,” per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

items.scope: “No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man”
items.why: This popular expanded version appears in none of the ancient sources; it is a modern paraphrase pinned onto Heraclitus, unlike the terse genuine fragments collected on Wikiquote.
The famous tag panta rhei does not appear in Heraclitus’s own fragments; it is a later label for his philosophy, as noted on Wikiquote.

misattribution.truthLine: Real doctrine, real philosopher — but the crisp “step twice” wording is Plato’s paraphrase, and Heraclitus’s own surviving river line (B12) reads differently. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Heraclitus’s river is one of the oldest and most quoted images in Western thought — a one-line argument that identity itself is unstable, because the thing you name (a river, a self) is really a process that never holds still. It seeded debates about change, persistence, and identity that run from Plato through Hegel to modern philosophy of time.

Ironically, the version everyone remembers is the one Plato used to caricature Heraclitus — sharpening “other and other waters flow” into “you could not step twice” to portray him as denying stable knowledge altogether.
context.detailsSummary: The three river fragments — and which one is genuine
detailsBody: Scholars distinguish three ‘river’ fragments: B12 (“other and other waters flow”), B49a (“into the same rivers we step and do not step”), and B91a (“it is not possible to step twice into the same river”). Only B12 has the linguistic density typical of Heraclitus; the “step twice” versions may derive, per Marcovich (1967), from a misreading of B12 — the very reading Plato popularized. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
